title: Car Loan Calculator — French Amortization (Fixed Payment) 2026
description: Calculate your fixed monthly car loan payment using the French amortization method. Enter loan amount, term, and annual rate — get the exact monthly payment, total paid, and interest cost instantly.
intro: Most auto loans worldwide use **French amortization**: your monthly payment is fixed for the entire term, but the split between interest and principal shifts every month — early payments are mostly interest, later ones mostly principal. Enter your loan amount, term in months, and annual interest rate to see your exact monthly payment, total cost, and how much you'll pay in interest.
keyTakeaway: With a **$25,000 loan at 7.5% APR over 60 months**, your monthly payment is **$500.95**, and you'll pay **$5,057 in total interest** — about 20% on top of the principal.
useCases: Budget how much car you can afford before visiting a dealership
Compare the true cost of a shorter 36-month term vs. a longer 72-month term

fields.label: Loan Term (months)

explanation:
## How French Amortization Works

The **French amortization system** (also called the *constant-payment* or *level-payment* method) is the standard loan structure used by banks, credit unions, and auto dealers in the US, Europe, and most of Latin America. The defining feature is that **your payment is identical every month** — no surprises.

What changes is the **internal split** between interest and principal:

- **Month 1**: Most of the payment is interest (because the full principal is still outstanding).
- **Final month**: Almost all of the payment is principal (because you've paid down the balance).

This is the opposite of the German (constant-principal) method, where payments start high and decrease.

## How to Calculate

### The PMT Formula

$$C = V \times \frac{i \cdot (1+i)^n}{(1+i)^n - 1}$$

Where:
- **C** = monthly payment
- **V** = loan principal (amount financed)
- **i** = monthly interest rate = Annual Rate (APR) ÷ 12 ÷ 100
- **n** = total number of monthly payments

**Special case**: if the interest rate is 0%, C = V / n (simple division).

### Month-by-Month Breakdown

For each month *k*:
- Interest portion = remaining balance × i
- Principal portion = C − interest portion
- New balance = old balance − principal portion

### Total Cost

- **Total paid** = C × n
- **Total interest** = Total paid − V

## Example: $20,000 at 6% for 48 Months

i = 0.06 / 12 = 0.005; (1.005)^48 = 1.2705

C = 20000 × 0.005 × 1.2705 / (1.2705 − 1) = 20000 × 0.006352 / 0.2705 ≈ **$469.70/month**

Total paid = $469.70 × 48 = $22,545.60 → interest = **$2,545.60 (12.7% of principal)**

## Why the Monthly Rate Is APR ÷ 12

This calculator uses the **nominal APR**, not APY (Annual Percentage Yield). The nominal rate is simply divided by 12 to get the monthly rate, matching how lenders in the US and most countries calculate installment loans. APY would compound the rate, producing a slightly different figure — use this calculator's result to cross-check any lender quote.

faq.q: What is French amortization and why is it used for auto loans?
faq.a: French amortization means every monthly payment is exactly the same dollar amount for the life of the loan. This makes budgeting easy and is the standard method used by US banks, credit unions, and most global lenders for auto financing. It contrasts with German-style loans where payments start high and decrease over time.

faq.q: Should I choose a 48-month or 72-month loan term?
faq.a: A 48-month loan has higher monthly payments but costs significantly less in total interest. A 72-month loan lowers the monthly payment but adds thousands in interest and increases the risk of being 'underwater' (owing more than the car is worth) due to depreciation. As a rule of thumb, financial advisors recommend keeping auto loans at 60 months or shorter.

faq.q: How does a bigger down payment affect my calculation?
faq.a: The down payment reduces the loan amount (V in the formula). For example, putting $5,000 down on a $30,000 car means you only finance $25,000 — lowering your monthly payment and the total interest you pay. Run the calculator with the financed amount after your down payment.

faq.q: What APR should I enter — the rate the dealer quoted or the one on the contract?
faq.a: Always use the APR shown on the loan contract or Truth-in-Lending disclosure, not the 'promotional rate' from an ad. Dealer finance departments sometimes quote a low APR that applies only to a portion of the loan or requires a short term. The contract APR is the legally binding figure.

faq.q: Why does early amortization show mostly interest, and late amortization mostly principal?
faq.a: Interest is always charged on the **remaining balance**. In month 1 you owe the full loan amount, so the interest charge is at its maximum. As you pay down principal over time, the balance shrinks, meaning interest charges shrink too — so more of your fixed payment goes toward principal each month.

faq.q: Can I pay off my car loan early to save on interest?
faq.a: Yes — prepaying reduces the remaining balance, so less interest accumulates afterward. The savings equal all the interest you would have paid on the portion of principal you eliminate early. Before prepaying, check your loan contract for **prepayment penalties**, which some lenders charge to recoup lost interest income.

faq.q: What is a good interest rate for a car loan in 2026?
faq.a: As of 2026, US average auto loan APRs from credit unions and banks typically range from 5% to 8% for borrowers with good credit (700+ FICO), and 10–20%+ for subprime borrowers. Dealership financing is often higher. The best strategy is to get pre-approved by your bank or credit union first, then compare with dealer offers.

faq.q: Does this calculator account for taxes, registration fees, or GAP insurance?
faq.a: No — this calculator computes the payment on the **financed amount** only. If taxes, fees, or add-ons (like GAP insurance) are rolled into the loan, add them to the loan amount field. If they are paid separately at purchase, exclude them.

faq.q: What is the difference between APR and APY for this calculation?
faq.a: APR (Annual Percentage Rate) is the nominal rate divided evenly across 12 months — this is what lenders use for installment loans and what this calculator expects. APY (Annual Percentage Yield) accounts for compounding and is used for savings accounts. For a standard car loan, always enter the APR.
